note.explanation: Efficiency compares the useful energy a system gives out with the energy put into it. Percentage efficiency is this ratio multiplied by 100. Some input energy is always wasted, so a real system cannot be 100% efficient.
examples: If useful output energy is 1200 J and input energy is 2000 J, efficiency = 1200/2000 = 0.6, or 60%.
A system with 100% efficiency would have output equal to input; your textbook calls this an ideal machine.
note.checkAnswer: Efficiency = (useful output energy / total input energy) × 100 = (300 J / 500 J) × 100 = 60%.
note.simple: Efficiency tells you what fraction of the input energy becomes useful output. Some energy is wasted, so the useful output is less than the input.

explain.title: What efficiency means
explain.body: The ratio of useful output energy and the total input energy is called the efficiency of a working system. Input energy is the energy available for conversion; output energy is the energy converted into the required useful form.

explain.title: Percentage efficiency
explain.body: To express efficiency as a percentage, multiply the ratio of useful output energy to total input energy by 100. It can also be calculated using useful power output and total power input.

explain.title: Why efficiency is below 100%
explain.body: Energy output is always less than energy input because some energy is wasted as heat during conversion. The losses in a working machine are inevitable, so a real system cannot have 100% efficiency.

explain.title: Perpetual energy machines
explain.body: A perpetual machine is hypothetical: it would work indefinitely without an external source of energy. This is impossible because it would have to produce energy from nothing, while real machines lose energy as heat through friction and air resistance.

mistakes: Reversing the ratio: use useful output energy divided by total input energy.
Using the slope distance to calculate useful gravitational potential energy; use the vertical height for mgh or wh.
Forgetting to multiply by 100 when the question asks for percentage efficiency.
Leaving out the percentage sign or mixing energy units in one calculation.
Claiming that a real machine can have 100% efficiency; some energy is always wasted as heat.
